comparisons.comparison: Both C and JPM disclose performance drivers for their card-related businesses in the U.S. consumer/retail segments, specifically focusing on how credit costs and partner dynamics impact non-interest revenue. C reports that Retail Services revenues increased 8% primarily due to 'lower partner payments, driven by the higher net credit losses,' indicating that worse credit performance reduced the fees paid to partners. JPM reports that Card income increased due to 'higher net interchange on increased debit and credit card sales volume,' but notes it was 'partially offset by an increase in amortization related to new account origination costs.' While both mention credit losses impacting partner payments (C explicitly, JPM implicitly via rewards costs in its 2025 context but focusing on interchange volume in 2024), the primary revenue driver for C was cost reductions from credit losses, whereas JPM's was volume growth, though JPM faced cost headwinds from origination amortization.

sentences.text: Retail Services revenues increased 8%, primarily driven by higher non-interest revenue due to the lower partner payments, driven by the higher net credit losses (see "Provisions" below and Note 5), as well as higher net interest income on growth in interest-earning balances.

Card income increased, reflecting higher net interchange on increased debit and credit card sales volume, as well as higher annual fees in CCB, partially offset by an increase in amortization related to new account origination costs.
